newsitem.title: INDIA: Indians vote in unsually peaceful polls in Punjab.
newsitem.headline: Indians vote in unsually peaceful polls in Punjab.

text.p: Polling began on an unusually peaceful note in India's northern state of Punjab on Friday amid tight security for the election of a new local government.
"This is the first time I have dared to vote in an election," said Shailendra Kumar, a 30-year-old car mechanic, as he waited for his turn at a voting booth in Ludhiana, Punjab's business hub.

Kumar, a Hindu, said his family was cautious about expressing their political opinions for fear of angering the state's Sikh separatists whose guerrilla war against Indian rule in Punjab killed more than 20,000 people in over a decade.
The last local election in 1992 to the 117-seat state assembly marked a new phase after the separatist rebellion, but was held in the shadow of guerrilla violence.
"Everyone knows that the political climate has changed dramatically, so we decided to cast our vote," Kumar said, looking at his family members in the small queue behind him.
"Polling has started on a peaceful note," Brajendra Singh, chief polling officer of Punjab, told Reuters in the state capital of Chandigarh.
"I am surprised at the enthusiasm of the voters as I have received reports of long queues at almost all polling stations before the voting started at 7.30 a.m. (0200 GMT)," Singh said.

Most opinion polls say the Akali Dal of former chief minister Prakash Singh Badal, which was once seen as flirting with separatists, would replace the Congress party's government in the polls. Results are expected by Sunday.

The party has an alliance with the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). "We are all set to rout Congress and give it its worst drubbing since independence," Balramji Dass Tandon, Punjab's BJP chief, told Reuters.
Polling stations are scheduled to close at 4.30 p.m. (1100 GMT). Around 15.2 million voters were eligible to vote, officials said.
Separatist violence peaked in 1984, when Indian troops were sent into Sikhism's holiest shrine, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, to flush out guerrillas armed to the teeth.

The army action triggered a bloody spate of violence in the state. Then prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two of her Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in what is believed to be a revenge killing for the army assault.
India has poured in 100,000 paramilitary soldiers to oversee elections. Police tightened security and sealed the borders of Punjab state with Pakistan.
Liquor shops and bars were closed for six days on the orders of the Election Commission. Politicians say liquor is used by activists to help violence or woo voters unfairly.

"Patrolling has been intensified. We are checking vehicles on suspicion and also conducting raids at known hideouts of Sikh and Kashmiri militants," state police chief Sube Singh said in Chandigarh, the state capital.
India's troubled Jammu and Kashmir state borders Punjab to the north. A still raging separatist revolt in Kashmir has led to 20,000 deaths since 1990.
India accuses Pakistan of arming Kashmir's Moslem militants. Islamabad, which disputes Kashmir, denies the charges.
The counting of ballots in Punjab is expected to start on Sunday and results are likely to be announced on the same day, officials said.
